Q: Excel - Find 2nd highest block average A:

Based on a range of A1:A21, array formula**:

=LARGE(IFERROR(SUBTOTAL(1,OFFSET(A1,3*(ROW(INDIRECT("1:"&INT(ROWS(A1:A21)/3)))-1),,3)),""),1)

Change LARGE's k parameter (1 here) as required.

**Array formulas are not entered in the same way as 'standard' formulas. Instead of pressing just ENTER, you first hold down CTRL and SHIFT, and only then press ENTER. If you've done it correctly, you'll notice Excel puts curly brackets {} around the formula (though do not attempt to manually insert these yourself).

Q: cv2 - Load grayscale Image as Numpy Array from Variable A:

import cv2

import numpy as np

import trimesh

# 1. Load the image and convert to grayscale

img = cv2.imread('map.jpg', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

img = cv2.resize(img, (500, 500)) # Resize for processing speed

# 2. Invert so lines/structures are elevated (high values)

img_invert = 255 - img

# 3. Create a 3D grid (Heightmap)

rows, cols = img.shape

x = np.arange(cols)

y = np.arange(rows)

xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y)

z = img_invert / 255.0 * 10 # Scale height extrusion depth

# 4. Generate Vertices

vertices = np.column_stack([xx.ravel(), yy.ravel(), z.ravel()])

# 5. Generate Triangles/Faces using vectorized NumPy (Fast)

r_idx, c_idx = np.meshgrid(np.arange(rows - 1), np.arange(cols - 1), indexing='ij')

idx = r_idx * cols + c_idx

# Upper-left triangles

faces_1 = np.column_stack([idx.ravel(), (idx + cols).ravel(), (idx + 1).ravel()])

# Lower-right triangles

faces_2 = np.column_stack([(idx + 1).ravel(), (idx + cols).ravel(), (idx + cols + 1).ravel()])

# Combine all faces

faces = np.vstack([faces_1, faces_2])

# 6. Create Mesh and Export to PLY

mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=vertices, faces=faces)

mesh.export('map_3d.ply')

print("Successfully saved map_3d.ply")

Q: How can I recreate my background I envisioned A:

You have chosen polygon shapes for the clip-path property. However, a polygon always has straight edges, not curvy ones. To generate curvy shapes as you envisioned, you will need a shape value defined by path() function.

mdn provides an explanation about its syntax at clip-paths CSS property - CSS | MDN

clip-path: path( "M0.5,1 C0.5,1,0,0.7,0,0.3 A0.25,0.25,1,1,1,0.5,0.3 A0.25,0.25,1,1,1,1,0.3 C1,0.7,0.5,1,0.5,1 Z" );

That particular shape is not your envisioned one, of course, it's just a demo of syntax. A shape is defined by path() function, which parameter is a string of SVG path. Inside the SVG Path is a sequence of "path commands", each with its own amount of parameters. They are:

  • M - move to
  • L - line to
  • H - horizontal line
  • V - vertical line
  • C - cubic Bézier curve, 2 control points
  • S - smooth Bézier curve, reusing the previous control point’s reflection
  • Q - quadratic Bézier curve, 1 control point
  • T - smooth quadratic Bézier curve
  • A - elliptical arc
  • Z - close the path

To write SVG paths by hand could be a daunting task. There are several on-line SVG shape editors to make it easier composing the paths. For instance, you can try SVG Path Editor , where you can draw the shapes (including curvy ones) and it will generate the associated SVG Path string so that you can copy to your own CSS definition. There are more sites like it, just google "SVG Path Editor" and find the one you feel the most comfortable to use.

Q: How can I apply tail/tails to a string of text in a Unicode-aware manner? A:

The text-icu package seems to be a thin wrapper around a C library. It's not even clear how to access the characters in Data.Text.ICU.Break, and they're all in the IO library.

However, once you've jumped that hurdle. probably the best way to handle this is with a fingertree. You'd write something like this:

import Data.FingerTree (FingerTree, Measured(..))
import qualified Data.FingerTree as F
import Data.Semigroup (Semigroup(..))
import qualified Data.Text as T
import qualified Data.Text.ICU.Break as B

data TSize = TSize {
    tCharacters :: {-# UNPACK #-} !Int,
    tGraphemes  :: {-# UNPACK #-} !Int
  } deriving (Eq, Show)

instance Semigroup TSize where
  TSize ca ga <> TSize cb gb = TSize (ca + cb) (ga + gb)

instance Monoid TSize where
  mempty = TSize 0 0

data Grapheme
  = Single {-# UNPACK #-} !Char
  | Cluster {-# UNPACK #-} !Text
  deriving (Eq, Show)

instance Measured TSize Grapheme where
  measure (Single _) = TSize 1 1
  measure (Cluster t) = TSize (T.size t) 1

newtype Clusters = Clusters { getClusters :: FingerTree TSize Grapheme }
  deriving (Eq)

toClusters :: LocaleName -> Text -> IO Clusters
toClusters = ...

And then you can use head or tail on it in O(1), as well as other benefits, like O(lg n) concatenation.
